domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
stem: A 56-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and ankle swelling over 6 months. His erect posteroanterior chest radiograph is shown. Which primary radiological abnormality is demonstrated, and which condition is a recognised underlying cause?
options: Hilar lymphadenopathy; pulmonary sarcoidosis
Left lower lobe collapse; endobronchial tumour
Pulmonary hyperinflation; severe emphysema
Marked cardiomegaly; dilated cardiomyopathy
Mediastinal widening; thoracic aortic aneurysm
optionRationales: Incorrect: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy appears as lobulated hilar fullness rather than global enlargement of the cardiopericardial silhouette.
Incorrect: Left lower lobe collapse produces a triangular retrocardiac opacity with ipsilateral tracheal or mediastinal shift and reduced left lung volume, rather than an enlarged cardiac shadow.
Incorrect: Pulmonary hyperinflation in COPD flattens the hemidiaphragms and elongates a narrow, vertical ('tubular') heart rather than causing cardiac enlargement.

Correct: The erect PA chest radiograph shows a cardiothoracic ratio greater than 0.50 (cardiomegaly), for which dilated cardiomyopathy, valvular heart disease, hypertensive heart disease, ischaemic heart disease, and pericardial effusion are classic causes.
Incorrect: The abnormality involves enlargement of the cardiac silhouette itself rather than the superior mediastinal vascular shadow typical of an ascending or arch aortic aneurysm.
clinicalPearl: In CSS chest X-ray stations, always confirm the film is an erect PA inspiratory view before calling cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio > 0.50), as AP projection magnifies the heart shadow by ~15–20%.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Cardiomegaly (CTR > 0.50 on PA CXR) caused by dilated cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, ischaemic/hypertensive heart disease, or pericardial effusion.

sourceStation.title: Cardiomegaly on Chest X-Ray
sourceStation.originalPrompt:

B.) List 3 causes.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Abnormality: Cardiomegaly. Causes: Dilated cardiomyopathy, Pericardial effusion, Valvular heart disease (e.g., mitral/aortic regurgitation), Hypertensive heart disease, Ischaemic heart disease.

domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
topic: Yellow Oleander Poisoning & Cardiac Glycoside Toxicity
stem: A 22-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Treatment Unit 4 hours after intentionally ingesting crushed yellow oleander (Thevetia peruviana) seeds. Three ECG traces (A, B, and C) are shown. Which trace and electrophysiological mechanism best represent the classic cardiac toxicity of this poisoning?
options: Trace A; Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition causing bradyarrhythmia and AV block
Trace B; beta-1 adrenergic stimulation causing sustained supraventricular tachycardia
Trace C; fast sodium-channel blockade causing sinus tachycardia and ST depression
Trace C; muscarinic receptor antagonism causing rapid atrial conduction
Trace B; potassium-channel blockade causing monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
optionRationales: Correct: Yellow oleander seeds contain cardiac glycosides that inhibit Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and increase vagal tone, classically producing sinus bradycardia, junctional escape rhythms, and variable or complete AV heart block as seen in Trace A.
Incorrect: Trace B shows a rapid tachyarrhythmia; yellow oleander does not stimulate beta-1 receptors and typically suppresses SA/AV nodal conduction.

Incorrect: Trace C shows a rapid narrow-complex rhythm with ST depression; although tricyclic antidepressants block fast sodium channels, cardiac glycosides cause AV nodal block and bradycardia rather than muscarinic tachycardia.
Incorrect: Antimuscarinic toxicity causes sinus tachycardia, whereas yellow oleander increases parasympathetic vagal tone at the SA and AV nodes.
Incorrect: Trace B is not characteristic of early oleander AV block, and cardiac glycosides do not act primarily via potassium-channel blockade to cause monomorphic VT.
clinicalPearl: Yellow oleander (kaneru) is a high-yield Sri Lankan toxicology emergency: monitor serum K⁺ closely alongside continuous ECG, as hyperkalaemia correlates strongly with severe AV block and mortality.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Yellow oleander (kaneru) cardiac glycosides inhibit Na+/K+-ATPase, producing bradycardia, AV nodal block, and hyperkalaemia.

sourceStation.title: Yellow Oleander Poisoning — ECG Selection
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
Q.2
A patient was brought to the ward with yellow oleander poisoning. Three ECG traces (A, B, C) are shown. What is the most likely ECG trace from him?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Trace A (Bradyarrhythmia / AV nodal conduction block). Cardiac glycosides in yellow oleander inhibit Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, classically causing sinus bradycardia, variable/complete AV heart block, and junctional escape rhythms (with hyperkalaemia).

domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
stem: A 58-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents to the Emergency Treatment Unit with crushing central chest pain radiating to the left arm and diaphoresis for 90 minutes. His 12-lead ECG is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute viral pericarditis with widespread repolarisation changes
Acute massive pulmonary embolism with right ventricular strain
Acute anteroseptal ST-elevation myocardial infarction
Isolated posterior wall myocardial infarction
Benign early repolarisation variant in precordial leads
optionRationales: Incorrect: Acute pericarditis causes diffuse upward-concave ST elevation across multiple territories without reciprocal ST depression (except in aVR/V1) and often shows PR-segment depression.
Incorrect: Pulmonary embolism typically produces sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3, right axis deviation, or anterior T-wave inversion (V1–V4) rather than convex territorial ST elevation.
Correct: The ECG shows marked convex ST-segment elevation in contiguous leads V1–V3 (with V4) accompanied by reciprocal ST depression in leads III and aVF, diagnostic of acute anteroseptal STEMI.
Incorrect: Isolated posterior MI presents with horizontal ST depression and tall R waves in V1–V2 (mirror image of posterior ST elevation) rather than prominent anterior ST elevation.
Incorrect: Benign early repolarisation features J-point notching and concave ST elevation mostly in V2–V5 in young healthy individuals without reciprocal inferior ST depression.
clinicalPearl: Look for reciprocal ST-segment depression in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF) to rapidly distinguish true anteroseptal STEMI from mimics such as pericarditis or early repolarisation, and initiate urgent reperfusion (primary PCI or thrombolysis).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Anteroseptal STEMI shows contiguous ST elevation in V1–V4 with reciprocal ST depression confirming acute coronary occlusion.

sourceStation.title: Acute ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) ECG
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
02. An ECG strip is given.
What is the diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI). Look for convex ST-segment elevation in contiguous territorial leads with reciprocal ST depression.

domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
topic: Erythema Marginatum in Acute Rheumatic Fever
stem: A 12-year-old boy presents 3 weeks after an untreated streptococcal pharyngitis with fever, migratory large-joint polyarthritis, and a new apical pansystolic murmur. Trunk examination shows transient, non-pruritic pink annular patches with raised serpiginous borders and central clearing. Which skin sign is present, and what condition does it indicate?
options: Erythema multiforme; herpes simplex virus infection
Erythema nodosum; primary pulmonary tuberculosis
Janeway lesions; acute staphylococcal infective endocarditis
Erythema chronicum migrans; disseminated Lyme borreliosis
Erythema marginatum; acute rheumatic fever
optionRationales: Incorrect: Erythema multiforme produces characteristic fixed 'target' (iris) lesions predominantly on the distal extremities and mucosa rather than transient serpiginous trunk rings.
Incorrect: Erythema nodosum presents as tender, violaceous subcutaneous nodules typically on the anterior shins rather than painless, spreading annular patches on the trunk.
Incorrect: Janeway lesions are painless haemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles seen in infective endocarditis, not annular serpiginous truncal patches.
Incorrect: Erythema migrans is typically a solitary expanding 'bull's-eye' plaque at a tick-bite site rather than multiple evanescent rings following streptococcal pharyngitis with carditis.

Correct: Erythema marginatum consists of evanescent pink rings with central clearing over the trunk and proximal limbs and is a Jones major diagnostic criterion for acute rheumatic fever (here accompanied by carditis and polyarthritis).
clinicalPearl: In Sri Lanka, chronic rheumatic heart disease remains a leading cause of acquired valvular disease; remember the five Jones major criteria (pancarditis, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules) and 3-weekly IM benzathine penicillin prophylaxis.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Acute rheumatic fever/carditis requires secondary prophylaxis with 3-weekly IM benzathine penicillin to prevent chronic valvular heart disease.

sourceStation.title: Erythema Marginatum (Acute Rheumatic Fever)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
03. Photograph of the chest with reddened round large annular patches (erythema marginatum).
What is the diagnosis?  [Chest photo omitted in 2013 archive files]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Erythema marginatum — a Jones major criterion seen in Acute Rheumatic Fever / Rheumatic Heart Disease (alongside migratory polyarthritis, pancarditis, subcutaneous nodules, and Sydenham chorea).

domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
stem: A 70-year-old man collapses in the Emergency Treatment Unit, becoming unconscious and apnoeic with an absent carotid pulse. The continuous cardiac monitor strip obtained immediately is shown. Which rhythm is present, and what is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Asystole; immediate intravenous adrenaline 1 mg and chest compressions without shock
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia; carotid sinus massage and intravenous adenosine
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with pulse; intravenous magnesium sulphate bolus
Atrial fibrillation with rapid response; urgent synchronised cardioversion at 50 J
Ventricular fibrillation; immediate high-quality CPR and unsynchronised DC shock
optionRationales: Incorrect: Asystole shows an isoelectric flat line and is non-shockable, whereas this trace displays coarse chaotic electrical activity requiring immediate defibrillation.
Incorrect: Monomorphic VT shows uniform wide QRS complexes, and vagal manoeuvres or adenosine are indicated only in stable regular supraventricular tachycardias, never in pulseless arrest.
Incorrect: The patient is unconscious with an absent carotid pulse (cardiac arrest), so magnesium monotherapy without immediate defibrillation and CPR is inappropriate.
Incorrect: Atrial fibrillation preserves narrow QRS complexes with irregular R-R intervals and a palpable pulse, unlike this pulseless arrest trace.

Correct: The strip demonstrates chaotic, irregular fibrillatory waves of varying amplitude with no identifiable QRS complexes (ventricular fibrillation), a shockable arrest rhythm treated with immediate CPR and unsynchronised DC defibrillation.
clinicalPearl: VF and pulseless VT are shockable arrest rhythms: deliver immediate unsynchronised biphasic DC shock (150–200 J) with minimal interruptions to 30:2 chest compressions, checking the carotid pulse only when organised rhythm returns.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Pulseless arrest with VF requires immediate 30:2 chest compressions and unsynchronised DC defibrillation after confirming absent carotid pulse.

sourceStation.title: Ventricular Fibrillation & Cardiac Arrest Management
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
3. A 70-year-old male patient admitted to the ETU unconscious and with absent carotid pulse. ECG strip shown.
1. What is the condition? (6 marks)
2. Write two initial management steps you take. (4 marks)
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Ventricular fibrillation (VF cardiac arrest). (2) Initial steps: Immediate Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR — chest compressions + airway/ventilation) and unsynchronised DC defibrillation (biphasic 150–200 J; note Drive key mentions 100 J).

domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
topic: Acute Anterior STEMI & Culprit Vessel Localisation
stem: A 62-year-old man develops sudden severe retrosternal chest pain and cold sweats. His 12-lead ECG is shown. Which combination of ECG abnormalities and likely culprit coronary artery best accounts for these findings?
options: Horizontal ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V2; left circumflex artery
Inferior lead ST elevation with reciprocal V1–V3 depression; right coronary artery
Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression; acute pericardial inflammation
Diffuse J-point notching in lateral leads; physiological early repolarisation
Precordial ST elevation with hyperacute T waves; left anterior descending artery
optionRationales: Incorrect: Posterior infarction causes anterior ST depression in V1–V2 rather than anterior ST elevation.
Incorrect: Inferior STEMI produces ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, whereas here lead III exhibits mild reciprocal ST depression and the primary elevation is anterior.
Incorrect: Pericarditis produces diffuse upward-concave ST elevation with PR depression rather than towering anterior ST elevation with hyperacute T waves.
Incorrect: Early repolarisation does not produce towering convex anterior ST elevation with hyperacute T waves in an acute chest pain presentation.

Correct: The ECG shows marked convex ST-segment elevation across the precordial leads (V2–V5, extending laterally to V6/I/aVL) with tall hyperacute T waves, diagnostic of acute anterior STEMI caused by left anterior descending (LAD) artery occlusion.
clinicalPearl: Hyperacute (tall, broad-based, symmetrical) T waves with precordial ST elevation represent the earliest hyperacute phase of anterior STEMI and mandate immediate cath-lab activation or thrombolysis without waiting for troponin elevation.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Precordial ST elevation across V1–V5 with hyperacute T waves localises an acute anterior STEMI to the LAD territory.

sourceStation.title: Acute Anterior STEMI ECG (V1–V5)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
04) Regarding the following ECG:
a) State 2 abnormalities you find.
b) What is the most probable diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (a) Abnormalities: ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V5 (precordial leads) and hyperacute/tall T waves (normal sinus rhythm ~75 bpm). (b) Diagnosis: Acute Anterior ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (Anterior STEMI).

domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
stem: A 25-year-old bank executive undergoes a routine pre-employment check-up and is completely asymptomatic, reporting no syncope, presyncope, or exertional dyspnoea. His 12-lead ECG is shown, and his transthoracic echocardiogram and baseline blood tests are entirely normal. What is the most appropriate clinical advice and follow-up plan?
options: Commence empirical intravenous amiodarone infusion followed by electrophysiological ablation
Reassure given the normal echocardiogram, arrange 24-hour Holter monitoring, and educate on syncope red flags
Initiate regular oral beta-blocker therapy to slow atrial conduction and prevent escape rhythms
Admit immediately for emergency temporary transvenous pacing and permanent pacemaker insertion
Start oral atropine prophylaxis and advise against all driving and strenuous activity indefinitely
optionRationales: Incorrect: Amiodarone slows AV nodal conduction and worsens bradyarrhythmias, and catheter ablation has no role in infra-nodal conduction delay.

Correct: In an asymptomatic young adult with first-degree AV block plus bifascicular block (RBBB + LAFB = trifascicular delay) and a normal echocardiogram, immediate pacing is not indicated; arrange 24-hour Holter monitoring/cardiology follow-up to rule out intermittent high-grade AV block and counsel on syncope or dizziness red flags.
Incorrect: Beta-blockers further depress SA and AV nodal conduction and are contraindicated in patients with existing bradycardia and conduction block.

Incorrect: Permanent pacing is reserved for symptomatic bradyarrhythmias, alternating bundle branch block, or documented Mobitz II/third-degree AV block rather than asymptomatic chronic trifascicular delay.
Incorrect: Chronic oral atropine is ineffective and toxic for distal His-Purkinje conduction delay, and permanent driving bans are unwarranted without syncope or high-grade block.
clinicalPearl: RBBB + left anterior fascicular block constitutes bifascicular block; adding a prolonged PR interval (>200 ms) is called trifascicular delay—always ask about syncope/presyncope and obtain a Holter monitor before considering pacing.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Asymptomatic trifascicular conduction delay (1st-degree AV block + RBBB + LAFB) with normal echo warrants Holter monitoring and red-flag counselling rather than immediate pacing.

sourceStation.title: Bifascicular / Trifascicular Block with Sinus Bradycardia (Routine Executive ECG)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
05) 25-year-old bank executive who underwent routine check-up shows the following ECG pattern (RBBB with 1st-degree heart block, sinus bradycardia). His echo and all other investigations were normal.
1) What is the diagnosis?
2) How would you advise him?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Diagnosis: Sinus bradycardia with trifascicular conduction delay (1st-degree AV block + Right Bundle Branch Block + Left Anterior Fascicular Block = bifascicular block + prolonged PR). (2) Advice: Reassure that in an asymptomatic young adult with a normal echocardiogram and normal baseline tests, isolated/asymptomatic conduction variants rarely need immediate intervention; advise 24-hour Holter ECG monitoring / cardiology follow-up to exclude intermittent high-grade AV block and educate on red-flag symptoms (syncope, presyncope, dizziness, exertional dyspnoea) requiring urgent review.

domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
stem: An asymptomatic 64-year-old man taking antihypertensive and glaucoma medications is noted to have a regular radial pulse of 44 bpm. His ECG rhythm strip is shown. Which rhythm is demonstrated, and which medication is a classic reversible cause?
options: Complete (third-degree) AV block; loop diuretic therapy
Idioventricular escape rhythm; dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker
Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block; inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist
Sinus bradycardia; systemic or topical beta-blocker therapy
Sinus arrest with junctional escape; angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor
optionRationales: Incorrect: Complete heart block shows AV dissociation with independent atrial and ventricular rates, whereas here P waves and QRS complexes maintain a fixed 1:1 relationship.
Incorrect: Idioventricular escape rhythms exhibit wide QRS complexes without preceding conducted P waves, and dihydropyridines (e.g., amlodipine) cause reflex tachycardia rather than AV/SA slowing.
Incorrect: Mobitz type I displays progressive PR prolongation culminating in a dropped QRS, and beta-2 agonists cause tachycardia rather than bradycardia.

Correct: The strip shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm at ~43 bpm with an identical upright P wave preceding every QRS complex at a constant normal PR interval (sinus bradycardia); beta-blockers (including timolol eye drops for glaucoma), verapamil/diltiazem, and digoxin are classic iatrogenic causes.
Incorrect: Every QRS is preceded by a normal sinus P wave at a constant PR interval (excluding junctional escape), and ACE inhibitors do not depress SA node automaticity.
clinicalPearl: In Sri Lankan outpatient clinics, always ask about glaucoma eye drops (topical timolol) alongside oral atenolol, carvedilol, verapamil, diltiazem, and digoxin when evaluating unexplained sinus bradycardia.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Sinus bradycardia has 1:1 P-to-QRS conduction at <60 bpm; exclude drugs (beta-blockers, verapamil, digoxin), inferior MI, and hypothyroidism.

sourceStation.title: Sinus Bradycardia ECG
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
2) Identify the ECG:
1) What is the diagnosis?
2) List 2 causes for it.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Sinus bradycardia (regular narrow-complex rhythm below 60 bpm with 1:1 normal P wave before every QRS). (2) Causes: Drugs (Beta-blockers, Verapamil/Diltiazem, Digoxin, Amiodarone), Inferior myocardial infarction (increased vagal tone / SA node ischaemia), Sick sinus syndrome, Hypothyroidism, Raised intracranial pressure (Cushing's reflex), Physiological (well-trained athletes / sleep), Electrolyte abnormalities (hyperkalaemia) / Hypothermia.

domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
stem: A 40-year-old man admitted with chest pain suddenly becomes unresponsive and stops breathing. His telemetry strip and two essential emergency trolley devices (A and B) are shown. Which option correctly identifies devices A and B along with their roles?
options: A is an automated ECG recorder; B is a continuous positive airway pressure mask for sleep apnoea
A is an external pacemaker for asystole; B is a metered-dose spacer for acute bronchospasm
A is a transcutaneous monitor for pulse oximetry; B is a non-rebreather mask for spontaneous breathing
A is a defibrillator for synchronised pacing only; B is a Venturi mask for fixed FiO₂ delivery
A is a defibrillator for unsynchronised DC shock; B is a bag-valve-mask for positive-pressure ventilation
optionRationales: Incorrect: Device A is equipped with external defibrillator paddles for therapeutic shock delivery, and Device B is an Ambu bag-valve-mask rather than a home CPAP mask.
Incorrect: Transcutaneous pacing is ineffective in VF arrest, and Device B is a manual resuscitator bag rather than an inhaler spacer.
Incorrect: Device A with heavy metallic paddles is a manual defibrillator, not a pulse oximeter, and Device B actively delivers manual breaths rather than relying on spontaneous inspiration.
Incorrect: Ventricular fibrillation requires an unsynchronised shock (synchronised shocks fail to trigger when no distinct R waves exist), and Device B is an Ambu bag rather than a Venturi mask.

Correct: The ECG shows ventricular fibrillation; Device A is a manual defibrillator (delivering an unsynchronised DC shock to depolarise myocardium and monitoring ECG), and Device B is a self-inflating bag-valve-mask (Ambu bag) providing positive-pressure ventilation with supplemental O₂.
clinicalPearl: On emergency trolley CSS stations, clearly state the distinction: use unsynchronised DC shock for VF/pulseless VT, synchronised cardioversion for unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse, and high-flow O₂ connected to the BVM reservoir.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Emergency trolley resuscitation relies on manual defibrillation (unsynchronised DC shock in VF) and bag-valve-mask (Ambu) positive-pressure ventilation.

sourceStation.title: Ventricular Fibrillation Arrest — Defibrillator & BVM
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
3. 40-year-old male admitted due to chest pain and suddenly became unresponsive and stopped breathing. His ECG and resuscitation equipment (A, B) are shown.
3.1 What is the diagnosis?
3.2 Identify A and B and state the purpose of each instrument.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (3.1) Ventricular fibrillation (cardiac arrest). (3.2) A: Automated/Manual Defibrillator — delivers controlled electrical shock (unsynchronised DC shock in VF/pVT) to depolarise myocardium and restore sinus rhythm; also monitors ECG. B: Bag-Valve-Mask (Self-inflating Ambu bag) — delivers positive-pressure ventilation (with high-flow O₂) in apnoeic or hypoventilating patients during resuscitation.

domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
stem: A 20-year-old man presents with progressively worsening shortness of breath, orthopnoea, and muffled heart sounds over 2 weeks. His posteroanterior chest radiograph is shown. What is the most probable diagnosis, and which bedside investigation confirms it?
options: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; serial arterial blood gas analysis
Tetralogy of Fallot; cardiac catheterisation and angiography
Descending thoracic aortic dissection; chest CT angiography
Large pericardial effusion; urgent bedside 2D transthoracic echocardiography
Massive left-sided pleural effusion; diagnostic pleural aspiration
optionRationales: Incorrect: Acute pulmonary oedema produces bilateral perihilar bat-wing alveolar infiltrates and Kerley B lines rather than clear, relatively oligaemic lung fields.
Incorrect: Tetralogy of Fallot characteristically produces a small 'boot-shaped' heart (coeur en sabot) with an upturned apex and pulmonary oligaemia rather than massive globular enlargement.
Incorrect: Thoracic aortic dissection widens the superior mediastinum and aortic knuckle rather than creating a symmetrical lower-mediastinal water-bottle silhouette.

Correct: The radiograph demonstrates a massive, symmetric globular ('water-bottle' / flask-shaped) cardiac silhouette with blunted chamber contours and relatively clear lung fields, typical of a large pericardial effusion; urgent bedside 2D echocardiography confirms fluid and evaluates for cardiac tamponade.
Incorrect: A large left pleural effusion causes homogeneous hemithoracic opacification with a rising lateral meniscus rather than a centrally positioned globular cardiac silhouette.
clinicalPearl: Always assess a 'water-bottle' heart clinically for Beck's triad (hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled heart sounds) and pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg inspiratory SBP drop), indicating life-threatening cardiac tamponade requiring urgent pericardiocentesis.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Globular 'water-bottle' cardiomegaly with clear lung fields suggests a large pericardial effusion; confirm urgently with 2D echocardiography.

sourceStation.title: Massive Cardiomegaly / Pericardial Effusion ('Water-Bottle' Heart) CXR
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
02. A 20-year-old boy presents with shortness of breath for 2 weeks.
1. List two abnormalities seen in the X-ray.
2. What is the most probable diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) CXR abnormalities: Markedly increased cardiothoracic ratio (globular/'water-bottle' cardiac silhouette) with loss of normal cardiac chamber contours and relatively oligaemic/clear lung fields. (2) Probable diagnosis: Large pericardial effusion (risk of cardiac tamponade; confirm urgently with bedside 2D echocardiography).

domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Treatment Unit with severe dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and an episode of breathlessness that woke her from sleep gasping for air. Which lung auscultation finding is most characteristic of her condition?
options: Diffuse high-pitched inspiratory stridor loudest over the upper trachea
Globally diminished vesicular breath sounds with prolonged expiration
Localised bronchial breathing with whispering pectoriloquy at the left apex
Bilateral fine inspiratory crepitations predominantly at the lung bases
Unilateral absent breath sounds with stony dullness at the right base
optionRationales: Incorrect: Inspiratory stridor indicates extrathoracic upper airway obstruction (e.g., croup, epiglottitis, or laryngeal oedema) rather than left heart failure.
Incorrect: Globally diminished breath sounds with prolonged expiration are typical of emphysema/COPD rather than acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
Incorrect: Localised bronchial breathing with whispering pectoriloquy reflects lobar consolidation rather than bilateral alveolar pulmonary oedema.

Correct: Orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea indicate left ventricular failure / acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, producing bilateral fine basal inspiratory crepitations (and occasionally expiratory wheeze, 'cardiac asthma', plus an S3 gallop).
Incorrect: Unilateral absent breath sounds with stony dullness indicate a large pleural effusion rather than acute left ventricular failure.
clinicalPearl: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea ('waking up breathless 1–2 hours after falling asleep and needing to sit upright') is a hallmark symptom of left ventricular failure; manage acutely with sitting upright, oxygen, IV frusemide, and IV nitrates if normo/hypertensive.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (LVF) presents with PND/orthopnoea and bilateral fine basal inspiratory crepitations.

sourceStation.title: Acute Pulmonary Oedema / Left Ventricular Failure Auscultation
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
1. 45-year-old woman presents with severe difficulty in breathing, complains of breathlessness at night and 1 episode of breathlessness that woke her up in the night.
What are the abnormal findings likely to be found in the auscultation of lung fields?  [Text-only clinical vignette station]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Bilateral fine inspiratory crepitations (crackles) predominantly at the lung bases (extending upwards with severity), possible expiratory wheeze ('cardiac asthma'), and reduced breath sounds at bases if pleural effusion coexists (plus S3 gallop rhythm on cardiac auscultation).

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 54-year-old man with chronic cough and weight loss has a posteroanterior chest radiograph showing homogeneous opacification of the right lower and mid zones with a concave upper meniscus and leftward tracheal shift. Which physical examination triad is expected over the affected right hemithorax?
options: Impaired percussion note, pleural friction rub, and increased vocal resonance
Stony dull percussion note, coarse inspiratory crackles, and ipsilateral tracheal shift
Stony dull percussion note, absent breath sounds, and reduced vocal resonance
Hyperresonant percussion note, absent breath sounds, and increased vocal resonance
Dull percussion note, bronchial breathing, and increased tactile vocal fremitus
optionRationales: Incorrect: Friction rubs and increased vocal resonance are not features over a large pleural effusion, which dampens sound transmission.
Incorrect: Large pleural effusions push the trachea and apex beat away from the affected side (contralateral shift); ipsilateral shift occurs in lung collapse or fibrosis.

Correct: A large right-sided pleural effusion produces reduced expansion, contralateral mediastinal shift (to the left), stony dullness to percussion, and absent/reduced breath sounds with diminished tactile vocal fremitus and vocal resonance.
Incorrect: Hyperresonance with absent breath sounds occurs in pneumothorax, not pleural effusion, and vocal resonance is reduced rather than increased.
Incorrect: Dullness (rather than stony dullness), bronchial breathing, and increased vocal fremitus characterise pulmonary consolidation with a patent bronchus, not fluid in the pleural space.
clinicalPearl: Just above the upper border (meniscus) of a pleural effusion, compressed lung parenchyma may yield a strip of bronchial breathing and aegophony ('bleating goat' quality); aspiration should be performed under ultrasound guidance or in the safe triangle.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Pleural effusion produces stony dullness, reduced expansion, absent breath sounds, reduced TVF/VR, and contralateral mediastinal shift.

sourceStation.title: Right-Sided Pleural Effusion CXR & Signs
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
03. Photograph of chest X-ray showing right-sided opacification of lung fields.
What is the radiological abnormality, and list 3 signs of this patient?  [CXR omitted in text-only 2012 archive PDF]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Abnormality: Right-sided pleural effusion. Signs: Reduced chest wall movement on right; trachea & apex beat shifted to left; reduced chest expansion and reduced tactile vocal fremitus on right; stony dullness to percussion; reduced/absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance (with bronchial breathing just above effusion level).

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 28-year-old man develops sudden severe left-sided chest pain, marked tachypnoea, hypotension (BP 78/46 mmHg), and distended neck veins in the Emergency Treatment Unit. An erect chest radiograph obtained before specialist review is shown. What is the immediate life-saving intervention?
options: Urgent endotracheal intubation followed by high-PEEP mechanical ventilation
Urgent contrast-enhanced CT thorax to exclude pulmonary thromboembolism first
Immediate intravenous frusemide 80 mg and non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation
Diagnostic needle pericardiocentesis via the left subxiphoid angle
Immediate wide-bore needle decompression in the left second intercostal space, midclavicular line
optionRationales: Incorrect: Intubation and high PEEP without prior pleural decompression sharply increase intrathoracic pressure and worsen obstructive shock.
Incorrect: Delaying decompression for CT imaging in haemodynamic collapse from tension pneumothorax can rapidly cause cardiac arrest.
Incorrect: Positive-pressure ventilation worsens air trapping and accelerates cardiovascular collapse in an undrained tension pneumothorax.
Incorrect: The mediastinal shift and collapsed left lung indicate air under tension in the left pleural space rather than pericardial tamponade.

Correct: Left-sided tension pneumothorax causes obstructive shock via mediastinal compression of venous return; per the CSS CXR guide, perform immediate wide-bore needle decompression in the left 2nd intercostal space at the midclavicular line (or 4th/5th ICS anterior axillary line per ATLS), followed immediately by an intercostal chest drain with underwater seal.
clinicalPearl: In real clinical practice, tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis (hypotension, raised JVP, absent unilateral breath sounds, hyperresonance, contralateral tracheal shift)—never wait for a CXR before performing needle decompression!

guideCitation.keyPoint: Tension pneumothorax requires immediate wide-bore needle decompression (2nd ICS midclavicular line) followed by an intercostal drain with underwater seal.

sourceStation.title: Left-Sided Massive / Tension Pneumothorax CXR
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
01. Photograph of an erect chest X-ray.
What is the diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Left-sided massive (tension) pneumothorax. Key features: radiolucent left hemithorax devoid of lung markings, visible visceral pleural edge, contralateral mediastinal shift to right, and flattened/depressed left hemidiaphragm.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
topic: Left Lingular Lobar Pneumonia & Silhouette Sign
stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of high fever, chills, and productive cough. His posteroanterior chest radiograph is shown. Which lobe or segment is consolidated, and what physical sign is expected over that region?
options: Right middle lobe; coarse basal crepitations with rightward tracheal deviation
Left lingula; dullness to percussion with bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance
Left pleural cavity; absent breath sounds with tracheal shift to the left side
Left upper lobe apex; hyperresonance with globally diminished vesicular breath sounds
Left lower lobe; stony dullness with absent breath sounds and reduced tactile fremitus
optionRationales: Incorrect: The opacity is in the left hemithorax obliterating the left cardiac border, not the right middle lobe.

Correct: The opacity obscures the left heart border while sparing the left hemidiaphragm (positive silhouette sign for the left lingula); lobar pneumonia produces dull percussion, increased tactile vocal fremitus, bronchial breathing, and increased vocal resonance.
Incorrect: A left-sided pleural effusion would cause leftward lung base meniscus and rightward (contralateral) tracheal shift rather than ipsilateral shift.
Incorrect: Apical consolidation spares the left heart border, and hyperresonance with diminished breath sounds indicates pneumothorax or emphysema rather than pneumonia.

Incorrect: Left lower lobe consolidation sits posteriorly behind the heart, leaving the left heart border crisp while obscuring the left hemidiaphragm, and consolidation does not cause stony dullness or absent breath sounds.
clinicalPearl: Master Felson's silhouette sign for CXR OSCEs: obliteration of the right heart border = right middle lobe; obliteration of the left heart border = left lingula; obliteration of either hemidiaphragm = the corresponding lower lobe.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Left lingular consolidation obliterates the left heart border (silhouette sign) and causes dullness, bronchial breathing, and increased TVF/VR.

sourceStation.title: Left Lingula Lobar Pneumonia CXR & Examination Signs
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
05) Person presented with 2-day history of fever. X-ray given.
1. What is the most likely diagnosis?
2. State 3 physical signs you find in the respiratory system examination.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Left lingular lobar pneumonia. (2) Signs: Reduced chest movement/expansion on left; increased tactile vocal fremitus; dullness to percussion over left mid-zone; bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance, and coarse crepitations over affected zone.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 29-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit following an accidental near-drowning episode. Examination reveals bilateral basal lung crepitations. On 100% inspired oxygen, his arterial blood gas shows PaO₂ 80 mmHg, and a bedside 2D echocardiogram is normal. What is the principal cause of his hypoxaemia, and which test confirms the pulmonary abnormality?
options: Acute pulmonary thromboembolism causing dead-space ventilation; D-dimer assay
Anaerobic bacterial lung abscess causing alveolar destruction; sputum Gram stain
Diaphragmatic splinting from gastric distension; supine abdominal radiograph
Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (ARDS) causing intrapulmonary shunting; chest radiograph
Acute left ventricular systolic failure causing pulmonary venous hypertension; serum BNP
optionRationales: Incorrect: While PE causes V/Q mismatch, hypoxaemia from dead-space mismatch usually responds partially to 100% O₂, unlike severe alveolar flooding/shunting after near-drowning.
Incorrect: Bacterial lung abscess develops subacutely over days to weeks and causes focal cavitation rather than acute bilateral basal crepitations immediately after submersion.
Incorrect: Gastric fluid distension does not account for bilateral basal crepitations and refractory shunting with a P/F ratio of 80 mmHg.

Correct: A PaO₂ of 80 mmHg on FiO₂ 1.0 yields a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 80 mmHg (<100 mmHg = severe hypoxaemia refractory to oxygen due to intrapulmonary shunting) with a normal echocardiogram excluding LV failure, diagnostic of near-drowning ARDS; CXR confirms bilateral alveolar infiltrates.
Incorrect: The completely normal 2D echocardiogram effectively excludes acute cardiogenic left ventricular systolic dysfunction.
clinicalPearl: Always calculate the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio when interpreting an ICU ABG: PaO₂ 80 mmHg looks acceptable on paper, but on FiO₂ 1.0 (100% O₂) the P/F ratio is 80 mmHg—indicating severe ARDS and intrapulmonary right-to-left shunting.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Always factor FiO2 into ABG oxygenation (P/F ratio); refractory hypoxaemia on 100% O2 with normal echo indicates non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (ARDS).

sourceStation.title: Near-Drowning Acute Pulmonary Oedema / ARDS
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
6. Patient admitted to the ICU due to incidental near-drowning. On examination, bilateral basal crepitations of lungs. ABG PaO2 80 mmHg with 100% O2. 2D echo normal.
1. What is the significant cause for hypoxaemia?
2. What is the investigation done to confirm it?  [Text-only station]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Acute pulmonary oedema (non-cardiogenic / ARDS) due to fluid aspiration (severe intrapulmonary shunting / V/Q mismatch). (2) Investigation: Chest X-ray (CXR) showing bilateral alveolar infiltrates.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 65-year-old chronic heavy smoker presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea and chronic productive cough. His lateral chest radiograph is shown. Which physical sign is most consistent with the underlying diagnosis?
options: Obliteration of cardiac and hepatic dullness with diminished breath sounds
Coarse late-inspiratory Velcro crackles with digital clubbing and low lung volumes
Dullness over the right apex with high-pitched bronchial breath sounds
Stony dull percussion note at both lung bases with reduced vocal resonance
Displaced heaving apex beat with bilateral fine basal inspiratory crackles
optionRationales: Correct: The lateral CXR demonstrates hyperinflation with increased retrosternal airspace, an increased anteroposterior chest diameter (barrel chest), and flattened hemidiaphragms typical of COPD/emphysema, causing global hyperresonance and obliteration of cardiac and liver dullness.
Incorrect: Fine/Velcro inspiratory crackles, clubbing, and reduced lung volumes are characteristic of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (restrictive), not obstructive hyperinflation.
Incorrect: Apical dullness with bronchial breathing suggests upper lobe pneumonia rather than generalised emphysema.
Incorrect: Stony dullness at the bases indicates bilateral pleural effusions rather than emphysematous pulmonary hyperinflation.
Incorrect: Cardiomegaly and fine basal crackles reflect left ventricular failure, whereas emphysema produces a narrow vertical heart and diminished breath sounds.
clinicalPearl: Classic CSS examination findings in emphysema include barrel-shaped chest, reduced cricosternal distance (<3 fingerbreadths), tracheal tug, loss of cardiac/liver dullness, and pursed-lip breathing (generating intrinsic PEEP to prevent airway collapse).

guideCitation.keyPoint: COPD/emphysema shows hyperinflation, flattened hemidiaphragms, and increased retrosternal space on lateral CXR, causing loss of cardiac/liver dullness.

sourceStation.title: COPD / Pulmonary Emphysema — Lateral CXR
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
1.
• Give 3 physical signs which can be elicited in the patient of the given CXR.
• What is the most likely diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Diagnosis: COPD / Pulmonary emphysema. Physical signs: Barrel-shaped chest (increased AP:transverse diameter), pursed-lip breathing / accessory muscle use, reduced cricosternal distance, hyperresonant percussion note globally, obliteration of cardiac/liver dullness, diminished breath sounds with prolonged expiration, and coarse/end-expiratory wheeze.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 66-year-old man with previously treated pulmonary tuberculosis presents with chronic cough, weight loss, recurrent haemoptysis, and fever for 2 months. Sputum Gram stain and AFB smears are negative. His chest radiograph is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Spontaneous tension pneumothorax with complete left lung collapse
Metastatic cannonball pulmonary deposits from renal cell carcinoma
Pulmonary aspergilloma colonising a pre-existing tuberculous cavity
Active miliary tuberculosis with haematogenous dissemination
Right upper lobe lobar pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion
optionRationales: Incorrect: A tension pneumothorax presents with a radiolucent hemithorax devoid of lung markings and contralateral mediastinal shift, neither of which is present.
Incorrect: Cannonball metastases are multiple smooth, rounded bilateral solid nodules of varying sizes, usually lower-zone predominant, without a crescentic air rim inside a cavity.

Correct: The chest radiograph reveals a rounded intracavitary opacity within a thick-walled left upper zone cavity capped by a superior crescent of air (Monad's / air-crescent sign), classic for an Aspergillus fumigatus fungal ball (mycetoma) colonising an old post-TB cavity.
Incorrect: Miliary TB shows uniform tiny (1–2 mm) millet-seed nodules throughout both lung fields rather than a solitary upper-zone fungal ball in a cavity.
Incorrect: The lesion is a well-demarcated left upper zone cavity with an intracavitary mass, not a right upper lobe homogeneous consolidation.
clinicalPearl: An aspergilloma (mycetoma) is a saprophytic colonisation (unlike invasive or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis) that moves to the dependent side on decubitus imaging and can cause life-threatening haemoptysis requiring bronchial artery embolisation or resection.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Well-defined upper-lobe post-TB cavity containing a mobile rounded opacity capped by an air crescent (Monad's sign) indicates pulmonary aspergilloma.

sourceStation.title: Pulmonary Aspergilloma (Mycetoma) CXR
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
7. 66-year-old man with a 2-year history of chronic cough, weight loss, and haemoptysis presents with fever for 2 months' duration. Sputum Gram stain does not reveal any bacteria.
What is the diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Pulmonary aspergilloma (fungal ball / mycetoma) colonising a pre-existing tuberculous cavity in the left upper zone.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
stem: During general examination of a 54-year-old man presenting with severe acute dyspnoea, the clinical appearance of the tongue and lips shown is noted. What is this physical sign, and what is its underlying mechanism?
options: Peripheral cyanosis; local arteriolar vasoconstriction with normal arterial oxygenation
Addisonian hyperpigmentation; excess melanocyte-stimulating ACTH secretion
Primary polycythaemia; increased erythrocyte mass without reduced oxygen saturation
Carbon monoxide toxicity; cherry-red discolouration from carboxyhaemoglobin
Central cyanosis; systemic arterial hypoxaemia with elevated deoxyhaemoglobin
optionRationales: Incorrect: Peripheral cyanosis affects cool acral extremities (fingers, toes, nose tip) due to sluggish peripheral flow while sparing the warm tongue and oral mucosa.
Incorrect: Addison disease causes patchy brownish-black melanin hyperpigmentation along buccal creases and gums rather than acute diffuse violaceous cyanosis.

Incorrect: Although polycythaemia lowers the threshold for cyanosis to become clinically visible, uncomplicated polycythaemia with normal arterial saturation causes plethora rather than central cyanosis.
Incorrect: Carbon monoxide produces carboxyhaemoglobin rather than bluish-purple cyanosis of the tongue.

Correct: Bluish-purple discolouration of a warm central mucous membrane (undersurface and dorsum of the tongue and lips) defines central cyanosis, caused by increased deoxyhaemoglobin in systemic arterial blood (typically >5 g/dL in capillaries) due to severe cardiopulmonary failure, right-to-left shunt, or methaemoglobinaemia.
clinicalPearl: Always inspect the undersurface of the tongue in good natural light to verify central cyanosis; remember that severe anaemia (Hb <5 g/dL) may mask cyanosis despite profound hypoxaemia because absolute deoxyhaemoglobin cannot reach 5 g/dL.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Central cyanosis affects the warm tongue and mucosa (reflecting arterial hypoxaemia/right-to-left shunt), distinguishing it from peripheral cyanosis.

sourceStation.title: Central Cyanosis (Tongue)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
9.1 What is the abnormality?
9.2 State one (01) possible cause for this abnormality.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (9.1) Central cyanosis. (9.2) Causes: Severe respiratory failure / COPD / pulmonary oedema / pneumonia, Cyanotic congenital heart disease (right-to-left shunt, e.g., TOF, Eisenmenger), Methaemoglobinaemia.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
topic: Right Upper Lobe Pneumonia CXR & Signs
stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with high fever and productive cough for 3 days. Her posteroanterior chest radiograph is shown. Which diagnosis and expected examination finding over the right infraclavicular area are most accurate?
options: Right upper lobe collapse; hyperresonant percussion note with leftward tracheal shift
Right upper lobe pneumonia; dull percussion note with bronchial breathing
Right-sided pleural effusion; stony dullness with absent vocal resonance
Right apical pulmonary abscess; amphoric breathing with normal tactile fremitus
Right tension pneumothorax; absent breath sounds with rightward apex shift
optionRationales: Incorrect: Right upper lobe collapse causes volume loss with upward bowing of the minor fissure and ipsilateral (rightward) tracheal deviation, and percussion over collapsed lung is dull rather than hyperresonant.

Correct: The radiograph shows homogeneous consolidation in the right upper zone bounded sharply below by the horizontal (minor) fissure without volume loss, diagnostic of right upper lobe pneumonia; examination yields impaired/dull percussion, bronchial breath sounds, coarse crepitations, and increased vocal resonance.
Incorrect: Pleural effusion collects dependently in the lower hemithorax with a curved meniscus rather than stopping cleanly at the horizontal fissure.
Incorrect: A lung abscess appears as a thick-walled cavity containing a horizontal air-fluid level rather than uniform lobar consolidation.
Incorrect: Pneumothorax produces an air-filled lucent pleural space devoid of lung markings rather than a dense homogeneous upper-zone opacity.
clinicalPearl: If right upper lobe consolidation displays a bulging, downward-convex minor fissure ('bulging fissure sign') in an alcoholic or diabetic patient, suspect Klebsiella pneumoniae and verify antibiotic coverage.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Right upper zone opacity bounded inferiorly by the horizontal fissure without volume loss indicates RUL lobar pneumonia with dullness and bronchial breathing.

sourceStation.title: Right Upper Lobe (RUL) Pneumonia CXR
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
2. A 45-year-old female presented to hospital with fever and productive cough for 3 days' duration. A chest X-ray was given.
2.1 Write three (03) physical signs you would elicit in the respiratory system to find the cause.
2.2 What is the most probable diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (2.1) Physical signs: Reduced expansion over right upper chest; increased tactile vocal fremitus; dull percussion note over right infraclavicular/supraclavicular area; bronchial breathing, coarse crepitations, and increased vocal resonance. (2.2) Diagnosis: Right upper lobe (RUL) lobar pneumonia.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 48-year-old woman complains of swinging fever and foul-smelling purulent productive cough for 2 months. Her chest radiograph is shown. What is the radiological diagnosis, and what is the cornerstone of initial medical management?
options: Right-sided hydropneumothorax; immediate intercostal tube drainage with underwater seal
Right middle lobe collapse; urgent fibreoptic bronchoscopy and chest physiotherapy alone
Right lung abscess; prolonged intravenous antibiotics covering anaerobes and Gram-positives
Ruptured pulmonary hydatid cyst; immediate surgical lobectomy without antibiotics
Pulmonary aspergilloma; oral itraconazole monotherapy without antibacterial agents
optionRationales: Incorrect: A hydropneumothorax spans the pleural cavity to the lateral chest wall with a long air-fluid level and visible pleural line rather than an intraparenchymal rounded thick-walled cavity.
Incorrect: Lobar collapse causes volume loss and fissure displacement rather than a cavitating air-fluid level, and requires investigation of obstruction rather than physiotherapy alone.

Correct: The chest radiograph reveals a thick-walled cavitating lesion in the right mid-zone containing a distinct horizontal air-fluid level surrounded by consolidation (lung abscess); initial treatment is prolonged empirical IV antibiotics covering anaerobes and Gram-positives (e.g., ampicillin-sulbactam or co-amoxiclav/clindamycin), tailored to cultures, with drainage reserved for failure.

Incorrect: Although ruptured hydatid cyst can mimic an air-fluid level ('water-lily sign' with floating membranes), a 2-month febrile purulent sputum course reflects a bacterial lung abscess requiring prompt antibiotic therapy first.
Incorrect: An aspergilloma presents as a solid rounded fungal ball inside an upper-lobe cavity with a crescent of air above it rather than a fluid-filled cavity with an air-fluid level.
clinicalPearl: In Sri Lankan OSCEs for lung abscess, remember predisposing causes (aspiration in alcoholism/stroke, bronchial obstruction/CA, Staph aureus post-influenza, Klebsiella) and ensure empirical anaerobic coverage (ampicillin-sulbactam or co-amoxiclav + metronidazole).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Thick-walled intrapulmonary cavity with a horizontal air-fluid level indicates lung abscess; treat initially with IV antibiotics covering anaerobes and S. aureus.

sourceStation.title: Right Lung Abscess CXR & Management
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
Question 02
48-year-old woman complains of fever and productive cough for a duration of 2 months.
2.1 What are the X-ray findings in this patient? (5 marks)
2.2 What are the treatment options for this patient? (5 marks)
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (2.1) Right lung abscess (fluid-filled cavity with an air-fluid level). (2.2) Management: (1) Empirical IV antibiotics covering anaerobes & Gram-positives (e.g., IV Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g 6-hourly, or IV Moxifloxacin / Levofloxacin + oral Metronidazole if penicillin-allergic), tailored to sputum/aspirate culture & ABST; (2) Percutaneous transthoracic or transbronchoscopic catheter drainage if failing medical therapy; (3) Surgical resection (lobectomy) if refractory/complicated.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 50-year-old man presents with fever, pleuritic chest pain, and productive cough for 5 days. His erect posteroanterior chest radiograph is shown. Which radiological abnormality is demonstrated?
options: Large right-sided tension pneumothorax collapsing the right lung
Right lower lobe consolidation obscuring the right hemidiaphragm
Left lingular consolidation obscuring the left cardiac border
Right upper lobe collapse elevating the horizontal fissure
Right middle lobe consolidation obliterating the right heart border
optionRationales: Incorrect: Pneumothorax causes hyperlucency devoid of lung markings rather than basal airspace consolidation.

Correct: The right lower zone displays patchy airspace opacity obscuring the contour of the right hemidiaphragm while leaving the upper zones clear, characteristic of right lower lobe consolidation (pneumonia).
Incorrect: The opacity is on the right side of the chest, whereas the left cardiac border and left lung field remain well aerated.
Incorrect: Right upper lobe collapse elevates the minor fissure toward the right apex and shifts the trachea ipsilaterally; the right upper zone is completely clear here.
Incorrect: Right middle lobe consolidation characteristically obliterates the right heart border while preserving the outline of the right hemidiaphragm.
clinicalPearl: Always look carefully at both hemidiaphragmatic domes and cardiac borders on PA CXRs: loss of the right hemidiaphragm localises consolidation to the right lower lobe rather than the middle lobe.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Right lower zone opacity obscuring the right hemidiaphragm localises consolidation to the right lower lobe.

sourceStation.title: Right Lower Lobe Consolidation (Pneumonia) CXR
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
02. This is a Chest X-ray of a 50-year-old male having fever for 5 days.
What is the radiological diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Right lower lobe (RLL) consolidation suggestive of pneumonia.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
topic: Peak Expiratory Flow Meter Identification & Indications
stem: The handheld respiratory device shown is routinely kept in medical clinics and emergency treatment units. Which instrument is this, and what is a primary clinical indication for its use?
options: Incentive spirometer; preventing postoperative basal atelectasis following laparotomy
Portable capnograph; measuring end-tidal carbon dioxide after endotracheal intubation
Peak expiratory flow meter; diagnosing asthma variability and grading acute exacerbations
Large-volume spacer chamber; trapping oversized aerosol droplets to prevent thrush
Dry powder inhaler; delivering daily inhaled corticosteroid maintenance therapy
optionRationales: Incorrect: An incentive spirometer uses floating balls or pistons during slow maximal inspiration to expand alveoli postoperatively, whereas a PEFM measures forced maximal expiration.
Incorrect: Capnography measures exhaled CO₂ waveform and partial pressure rather than peak expiratory airflow rate.

Correct: The instrument shown is a mini-Wright Peak Expiratory Flow Meter (scale 60–800 L/min), used to diagnose asthma (diurnal PEF variability >20% or bronchodilator reversibility), monitor control, and objectively grade acute asthma exacerbation severity.
Incorrect: A spacer is a hollow holding chamber attached to a pressurised metered-dose inhaler rather than a spring-loaded flow meter.
Incorrect: Dry powder inhalers (e.g., Turbuhaler, Diskus) are breath-actuated medication delivery devices rather than calibrated L/min airflow gauges.
clinicalPearl: Remember British/Sri Lankan acute asthma PEF thresholds: 50–75% predicted/best = moderate exacerbation; 33–50% = acute severe asthma; <33% = life-threatening asthma.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Peak expiratory flow meters measure maximal expiratory airflow (L/min) to diagnose diurnal asthma variability (>20%) and grade acute exacerbation severity.

sourceStation.title: Peak Expiratory Flow Meter (Wright PEFM)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
04.
1. Identify this instrument.
2. Write two indications for using this instrument.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Peak Expiratory Flow Meter (PEFM). (2) Indications: (a) Diagnosis of bronchial asthma (demonstrating diurnal PEF variability > 20% or bronchodilator reversibility); (b) Objective monitoring of asthma control, response to therapy, and grading severity of acute asthma exacerbations (predicted/personal best %).

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
topic: Peak Expiratory Flow Rate Measurement & Interpretation
stem: A 24-year-old woman with episodic nocturnal wheezing is asked to record twice-daily measurements using the colour-zoned device shown. Which measurement technique and diagnostic criterion are correct?
options: Record the highest of three maximal forced expiratory blows; diurnal variability >20% supports asthma
Stand upright, flex the neck fully, and take one gentle puff; diurnal dip <5% confirms asthma
Exhale steadily over 6 seconds with nose clipped; a value >80% predicted excludes asthma
Record the mean of three slow vital capacity exhalations; FEV₁/FVC <0.70 confirms asthma
Inhale sharply through the mouthpiece against resistance; a 12% fall confirms emphysema
optionRationales: Correct: Using the Peak Expiratory Flow Meter, the patient takes a full inspiration, seals lips tightly around the mouthpiece with the cursor reset to zero, and blows out as hard and fast as possible; the best of three attempts is recorded, and diurnal variability >20% ('morning dipping') supports bronchial asthma.
Incorrect: Flexing the neck narrows upper airway calibre and reduces flow, a gentle blow underestimates PEF, and normal diurnal variation is small (<10%), whereas >20% indicates asthma.
Incorrect: Because asthma is characterised by variable airflow obstruction, a normal inter-ictal PEF >80% predicted does not exclude asthma.
Incorrect: PEFM measures peak forced expiratory flow rate (best of three efforts), not slow vital capacity or spirometric FEV₁/FVC ratio.
Incorrect: PEFM requires forceful expiration after full inspiration (TLC), not sharp inhalation (which is used for dry powder inhalers).
clinicalPearl: In OSCE demonstrations of the Peak Flow Meter, never forget the 5 marking steps: reset pointer to zero, hold horizontally without blocking the slot, maximal inspiration, tight lip seal with short forceful blast, and take the highest of 3 readings.

guideCitation.keyPoint: PEFR requires resetting the pointer to zero, maximal inspiration, and a short forceful blast; record the best of 3 tries and look for >20% diurnal variability.

sourceStation.title: Peak Expiratory Flow Meter — Identification & Uses
sourceStation.originalPrompt: 2. Identify & write down the uses of the equipment given below.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Peak Expiratory Flow Meter. Used to measure Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR) for diagnosing bronchial asthma (diurnal variability/reversibility), monitoring disease control and occupational asthma, assessing acute asthma exacerbation severity, and evaluating response to bronchodilator/steroid treatment.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
topic: Right Lower Lobe Consolidation Respiratory Signs
stem: A 44-year-old man presents with dyspnoea and high fever for 5 days. His posteroanterior chest radiograph is shown. Which set of physical signs is most likely to be elicited over the posterior right lung base?
options: Stony dull percussion note, reduced tactile vocal fremitus, and absent breath sounds
Dull percussion note, leftward tracheal deviation, and decreased vocal resonance
Dull percussion note, increased tactile vocal fremitus, and whispering pectoriloquy
Resonant percussion note, bilaterally equal chest movement, and normal vesicular sounds
Hyperresonant percussion note, absent tactile vocal fremitus, and diminished breath sounds
optionRationales: Incorrect: Stony dullness, reduced TVF, and absent breath sounds characterise a pleural effusion rather than parenchymal consolidation.
Incorrect: Consolidation does not shift the trachea contralaterally and increases rather than decreases vocal resonance.

Correct: The radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation; consolidated lung with a patent bronchus conducts high-frequency vibrations efficiently, producing impaired/dull percussion, increased tactile vocal fremitus, bronchial breathing, coarse crepitations, and increased vocal resonance / whispering pectoriloquy.
Incorrect: Normal vesicular sounds and full resonance would be expected over healthy aerated lung rather than an extensive right basal consolidation.
Incorrect: Hyperresonance and absent TVF occur in pneumothorax rather than lobar consolidation.
clinicalPearl: Remember why consolidation gives bronchial breathing and whispering pectoriloquy while effusion does not: fluid-filled alveoli around a patent bronchus act as a solid acoustic bridge, whereas pleural fluid interposes an acoustic barrier.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Consolidation with a patent bronchus yields dullness (not stony), increased TVF, bronchial breathing, coarse crackles, and whispering pectoriloquy.

sourceStation.title: Right Lower Lobe Consolidation CXR — Respiratory Signs
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
2. A patient presented with difficulty in breathing. He had fever for 5 days.
List 4 physical signs you could elicit in respiratory system examination of this patient.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Inspection: Reduced chest movement on right lower hemithorax. (2) Palpation: Reduced lung expansion on right; increased tactile vocal fremitus over right base; central trachea. (3) Percussion: Dullness over right lower zone. (4) Auscultation: Bronchial breath sounds, coarse crepitations, and increased vocal resonance (or whispering pectoriloquy) over right base.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
stem: The bedside monitoring device shown is applied to a patient's index finger in the Emergency Treatment Unit. Which pair of clinical parameters does this device measure, and which condition causes a falsely normal saturation reading despite tissue hypoxia?
options: Arterial partial pressure of oxygen and respiratory rate; acute bronchial asthma
Central venous oxygen saturation and blood pressure; hypovolaemic shock
Peripheral arterial oxygen saturation and blood pH; diabetic ketoacidosis
Peripheral arterial oxygen saturation and pulse rate; carbon monoxide poisoning
End-tidal carbon dioxide and pulse rate; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
optionRationales: Incorrect: Pulse oximetry measures percentage haemoglobin saturation (SpO₂), not arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO₂, which requires an ABG) or respiratory rate.
Incorrect: Central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO₂) requires a central venous blood gas sample, and oximetry does not measure arterial blood pressure.
Incorrect: Blood pH cannot be measured non-invasively by finger spectrophotometry.

Correct: A pulse oximeter measures peripheral arterial oxygen saturation (SpO₂, %) and pulse rate (bpm); in carbon monoxide poisoning, carboxyhaemoglobin absorbs red light similarly to oxyhaemoglobin, producing a falsely reassuring SpO₂ despite severe functional hypoxaemia.
Incorrect: End-tidal CO₂ is measured via exhaled gas capnography rather than a fingertip photoplethysmograph.
clinicalPearl: Key pulse oximetry pitfalls for CSS vivas: carboxyhaemoglobin reads falsely normal, methaemoglobinaemia trends SpO₂ toward ~85%, and poor perfusion, cold peripheries, movement, or dark nail polish degrade the pulsatile signal.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Pulse oximetry estimates SpO2 and pulse rate, cannot measure PaCO2/pH, and reads falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning.

sourceStation.title: Pulse Oximeter
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
3.1 Identify the device.
3.2 List two parameters you could measure using this.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (3.1) Pulse oximeter. (3.2) Parameters: Peripheral arterial oxygen saturation (SpO₂, %) and pulse rate (heart rate, bpm) (plus plethysmographic perfusion index/waveform on clinical monitors).

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Complete Left Oculomotor (CN III) Nerve Palsy
stem: A 56-year-old woman presents with sudden severe headache and drooping of her left upper eyelid. Examination at rest (b) and with the left upper eyelid manually lifted (a) is shown. What is the cranial nerve lesion, and which urgent life-threatening cause must be excluded immediately?
options: Complete left oculomotor (CN III) palsy; posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Left Horner syndrome; apical bronchial carcinoma invading the stellate ganglion
Left abducens (CN VI) palsy; idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Left trochlear (CN IV) palsy; dorsal midbrain lacunar infarction
Complete left oculomotor (CN III) palsy; diabetic microvascular mononeuropathy
optionRationales: Correct: Lifting the completely ptotic left eyelid reveals a 'down-and-out' eye (unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique) plus a dilated left pupil (mydriasis from parasympathetic Edinger-Westphal fibre involvement); a painful pupil-involving ('surgical') CN III palsy is a posterior communicating (PCom) artery aneurysm until proven otherwise by urgent CTA/MRA.
Incorrect: Horner syndrome causes partial ptosis (1–2 mm) and miosis (constricted pupil) rather than complete ptosis, exotropia, and mydriasis.
Incorrect: Left CN VI palsy causes failure of abduction (esotropia) without ptosis or mydriasis.
Incorrect: Trochlear nerve palsy causes vertical/torsional diplopia and hypertropia worsened on downward medial gaze without complete ptosis or mydriasis.

Incorrect: Microvascular ischaemia from diabetes or hypertension affects the central vasa nervorum while sparing the superficial pial-supplied parasympathetic fibres, typically presenting as a pupil-sparing ('medical') CN III palsy.
clinicalPearl: Rule of the pupil in CN III palsy: parasympathetic pupillomotor fibres travel superficially in the dorsomedial nerve—external compression (PCom aneurysm, uncal herniation) involves the pupil ('surgical third'), whereas microvascular ischaemia usually spares it.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Complete pupil-involving CN III palsy (ptosis, down-and-out globe, mydriasis) demands urgent neuroimaging to rule out a PCom aneurysm or uncal herniation.

sourceStation.title: Complete Left 3rd Cranial Nerve (Oculomotor) Palsy
sourceStation.originalPrompt:

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (A) Complete left 3rd cranial nerve (oculomotor) palsy ('complete' because parasympathetic pupillary fibres are also involved → mydriasis, alongside lateral/downward deviation and ptosis). (B) Causes: Posterior communicating artery (PCom) aneurysm (surgical cause — pupil-involving!), Uncal herniation, Cavernous sinus thrombosis/tumour, Basal meningitis, Microvascular ischaemia (DM/HTN — usually pupil-sparing).

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Babinski Sign & Lower Limb UMN Physical Signs
stem: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive bilateral leg weakness and urinary urgency over 3 weeks. Eliciting the plantar response on his right foot demonstrates the finding shown in the right panel. Which combination of additional physical signs is expected in the same lower limb?
options: Clasp-knife spasticity, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and ankle clonus
Flaccid hypotonia, absent deep tendon reflexes, and prominent fasciculations
Hypotonia, pendular knee jerk, and intention tremor on heel-shin testing
Severe distal sensory ataxia, absent ankle jerks, and pes cavus deformity
Lead-pipe rigidity, pill-rolling resting tremor, and normal plantar responses
optionRationales: Correct: An extensor plantar response (upgoing great toe with fanning of the other toes) indicates a corticospinal upper motor neuron (UMN) tract lesion, accompanied by pyramidal weakness, clasp-knife spasticity, hyperreflexia, ankle/patellar clonus, and absent superficial abdominal reflexes.
Incorrect: Flaccidity, areflexia, and fasciculations are lower motor neuron (LMN) signs rather than UMN pyramidal tract signs.
Incorrect: Hypotonia, pendular reflexes, and dysmetria/intention tremor indicate ipsilateral cerebellar hemisphere dysfunction.
Incorrect: Absent ankle jerks and distal sensory ataxia indicate a peripheral neuropathy or dorsal column/LMN disorder rather than an isolated UMN lesion.
Incorrect: Lead-pipe rigidity and resting tremor represent extrapyramidal nigrostriatal dysfunction rather than a corticospinal lesion.
clinicalPearl: Remember the physiological exceptions where an extensor plantar response does NOT indicate UMN pathology: infants under 1 year (incomplete corticospinal myelination), deep sleep, general anaesthesia, post-ictal state, and profound hypoglycaemia.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Corticospinal (UMN) tract lesions produce an extensor plantar response alongside clasp-knife spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and pyramidal weakness.

sourceStation.title: Babinski Sign (Extensor Plantar Response)

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Sign: Positive Babinski sign (extensor plantar response) indicating Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) lesion. Conditions: Stroke (CVA), Spinal cord injury/compression, Multiple sclerosis (also physiological in infants below 1 year, deep sleep, general anaesthesia, severe hypoglycaemia). Other lower limb UMN signs: Muscle weakness (pyramidal pattern), Spasticity (clasp-knife hypertonia), Exaggerated deep tendon reflexes (hyperreflexia), Ankle/patellar clonus, Absent superficial abdominal reflexes.

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Bell's Palsy vs Ramsay Hunt & LMN CN VII Aetiology
stem: A 32-year-old woman awakens with acute-onset paralysis of both the upper and lower left face, incomplete left eye closure, and reduced taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on the left. Otoscopy shows a normal tympanic membrane and pinna with no vesicles. What is the most likely diagnosis and underlying cause?
options: Left upper motor neuron facial palsy; acute right internal capsule lacunar infarct
Left Ramsay Hunt syndrome; reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the pinna
Left trigeminal motor neuropathy; demyelination within the cavernous sinus
Left Bell's palsy; reactivation of herpes simplex virus type 1 in the geniculate ganglion
Ocular myasthenia gravis; autoantibodies blocking postsynaptic nicotinic receptors
optionRationales: Incorrect: An upper motor neuron facial palsy spares the ipsilateral forehead due to bilateral cortical innervation and does not abolish anterior-tongue taste via the chorda tympani.
Incorrect: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) presents with painful vesicular eruptions in the external auditory canal, pinna, or soft palate alongside severe otalgia.
Incorrect: Trigeminal (CN V3) motor neuropathy weakens mastication muscles (masseter/temporalis) rather than muscles of facial expression or taste.

Correct: Acute unilateral LMN facial nerve palsy (involving forehead and taste via chorda tympani) without external ear vesicles or focal CNS signs is idiopathic Bell's palsy, classically triggered by HSV-1 reactivation causing inflammatory swelling of CN VII within the bony facial canal.
Incorrect: Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable ocular/bulbar weakness without sensory taste impairment and typically spares deep facial nerve reflexes.
clinicalPearl: Always examine the external auditory canal, tympanic membrane, and parotid gland in every patient with LMN facial palsy to avoid missing Ramsay Hunt syndrome (needs aciclovir + steroids) or a parotid malignancy.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Idiopathic LMN CN VII palsy (Bell's palsy, linked to HSV-1) affects the entire ipsilateral half of the face and must be distinguished from Ramsay Hunt (ear vesicles) and UMN lesions (forehead-sparing).

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Left LMN Facial Nerve Palsy & Bell's Phenomenon
stem: A 26-year-old man attends the neurology clinic and is asked to close both eyes tightly and show his teeth, producing the appearance shown. What is the diagnosis, and what accounts for the appearance of his left eye?
options: Right lower motor neuron CN VII palsy; unopposed contraction of the left orbicularis oris
Left lower motor neuron CN VII palsy; paralysis of orbicularis oculi exposing physiological Bell's phenomenon
Left oculomotor (CN III) palsy; paralysis of the inferior rectus muscle causing upward gaze
Left upper motor neuron CN VII palsy; preserved bilateral cortical drive to the left eyelid
Right upper motor neuron CN VII palsy; selective sparing of the lower facial musculature
optionRationales: Incorrect: The right eye closes firmly and the mouth is drawn toward the intact right side, proving the right facial nerve is normal and the left side is paralysed.

Correct: Incomplete left eyelid closure allows the normal physiological upward rolling of the globe on attempted lid closure (Bell's phenomenon) to become visible, while unopposed intact right facial muscles pull the mouth toward the right—classic for left LMN CN VII palsy.
Incorrect: CN III palsy causes ptosis (drooping) and downward-outward globe deviation rather than lagophthalmos with mouth deviation.
Incorrect: In an upper motor neuron lesion, upper facial muscles (orbicularis oculi and frontalis) are largely spared due to bilateral corticobulbar projections.
Incorrect: UMN lesions affect the contralateral *lower* face while sparing the upper face, and here the left eye fails to close while the mouth pulls right.
clinicalPearl: Bell's phenomenon (upward and outward rotation of the eyeball during attempted eye closure) is a normal protective reflex that only becomes visible when orbicularis oculi is paralysed in an LMN CN VII palsy.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Left LMN CN VII palsy causes incomplete left eye closure (exposing Bell's phenomenon) and unopposed pull of the mouth toward the intact right side.

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with the resting hand posture shown following a deep anterior laceration at the medial wrist. Which nerve lesion causes this abnormality, and why is the finger deformity more pronounced here than after an injury at the elbow?
options: Proximal radial nerve lesion; unopposed forearm flexors pull the ring and little fingers down
Distal median nerve lesion; lateral two lumbricals are paralysed with preserved flexor pollicis longus
Upper brachial plexus (C5–C6) lesion; unopposed pronators flex the medial interphalangeal joints
Proximal ulnar nerve lesion; flexor digitorum superficialis to the 4th and 5th digits is paralysed
Distal ulnar nerve lesion; flexor digitorum profundus to the 4th and 5th digits remains intact
optionRationales: Incorrect: Radial nerve lesions produce wrist drop and finger drop at the MCP joints rather than MCP hyperextension with selective 4th–5th IP flexion.

Incorrect: A distal median nerve lesion causes thenar wasting ('ape hand') and clawing/inability to flex the lateral digits on attempted fist ('hand of benediction'), not resting ring-and-little-finger clawing.

Incorrect: Upper trunk (C5–C6) lesions produce Erb's palsy ('waiter's tip' shoulder adduction/internal rotation and forearm pronation), whereas lower trunk (C8–T1) causes total claw hand (Klumpke's palsy).
Incorrect: A proximal ulnar lesion at the elbow additionally paralyses the medial half of FDP, resulting in *less* prominent clawing at the IP joints, and FDS is innervated by the median nerve.

Correct: A distal ulnar nerve lesion (at the wrist/Guyon's canal) paralyses the medial two lumbricals and interossei—causing MCP hyperextension via extensor digitorum—while sparing the proximal branches to flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) of the ring and little fingers, which pulls the IP joints into marked flexion ('ulnar paradox').
clinicalPearl: The 'ulnar paradox' is a favourite Kelaniya CSS viva question: the more distal the ulnar nerve injury (wrist), the worse the clawing, because the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (innervated in the forearm) remains intact to flex the DIP/PIP joints.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Distal ulnar nerve palsy produces worse clawing than a proximal elbow lesion ('ulnar paradox') because forearm innervation of medial FDP is preserved.
