sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Ulnar claw hand — due to lower (distal) ulnar nerve lesion (below elbow, e.g., Guyon's canal/wrist), causing paralysis of medial two lumbricals and interossei while flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) to ring & little fingers remains intact ('ulnar paradox').

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Complete Right Ptosis & Levator Palpebrae Paralysis
stem: An elderly man is asked to look straight ahead during a cranial nerve examination, showing the unilateral eyelid finding on the right. Which muscle paralysis produces this complete eyelid droop, and what is the most consistent cranial nerve lesion?
options: Frontalis; left upper motor neuron facial (CN VII) nerve lesion
Levator palpebrae superioris; right oculomotor (CN III) nerve palsy
Superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle; right oculosympathetic Horner syndrome
Superior oblique; right trochlear (CN IV) nerve palsy
Orbicularis oculi; right lower motor neuron facial (CN VII) nerve palsy
optionRationales: Incorrect: Frontalis elevates the eyebrow and assists eyelid elevation only weakly; UMN CN VII palsy spares the upper face and never causes complete unilateral ptosis.
Correct: Complete ptosis (eyelid completely obscuring the pupil) results from paralysis of the striated levator palpebrae superioris, which is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
Incorrect: Sympathetic denervation of the smooth-muscle superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle in Horner syndrome produces only mild partial ptosis (1–2 mm) accompanied by miosis and anhidrosis.
Incorrect: The trochlear nerve innervates only the superior oblique extraocular muscle and does not elevate the upper eyelid.
Incorrect: Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids; its paralysis in CN VII palsy causes lagophthalmos (inability to close the eye) rather than ptosis.
clinicalPearl: Always distinguish complete ptosis (CN III palsy—levator palpebrae superioris), partial ptosis with miosis (Horner syndrome—Müller's muscle), and variable fatigable ptosis (myasthenia gravis) during neurological spotter stations.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Complete ptosis reflects levator palpebrae superioris paralysis (CN III), whereas Horner syndrome causes partial ptosis (1–2 mm) from Müller's muscle denervation.

sourceStation.title: Right Complete Ptosis (Oculomotor Nerve Palsy)

(2) Causes: CN III palsy (PCom aneurysm, microvascular diabetes/hypertension, cavernous sinus lesion, midbrain stroke), Congenital/aponeurotic ptosis, Myasthenia gravis, Trauma.

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 58-year-old man presents with mild dysarthria. When asked to protrude his tongue straight forward, the appearance shown is observed. Which cranial nerve and side are affected, and why does the tongue deviate in this direction?
options: Left vagus (CN X) nerve; unopposed action of the intact right palatoglossus muscle
Right hypoglossal (CN XII) nerve; ipsilateral atrophy shortening the right tongue border
Right hypoglossal (CN XII) nerve; unopposed pull of the intact left styloglossus muscle
Left trigeminal mandibular (CN V3) branch; unopposed action of the right lateral pterygoid
Left hypoglossal (CN XII) nerve; unopposed push of the intact right genioglossus muscle
optionRationales: Incorrect: CN X palsy causes palatal droop and uvular deviation away from the paralysed side, not tongue protrusion deviation.
Incorrect: On protrusion, the tongue points toward the paralysed side (here the patient's left, not right).
Incorrect: The patient's tongue deviates to the patient's left (viewer's right), indicating a left-sided lesion rather than a right-sided one.
Incorrect: CN V3 lesions cause the opened *jaw* to deviate toward the weak side via unopposed contralateral lateral pterygoid, whereas tongue protrusion tests CN XII.

Correct: The protruded tongue deviates toward the patient's left side (viewer's right) with subtle left-sided wasting/furrowing; because each genioglossus pushes the tongue forward and contralaterally, a left LMN CN XII lesion allows the intact right genioglossus to push the tongue tip toward the paralysed left side.
clinicalPearl: Remember the universal rule for CSS cranial nerve exams: 'The tongue licks the lesion' (CN XII deviates toward the weak side), whereas 'the uvula flees the lesion' (CN X deviates away toward the intact side).

guideCitation.keyPoint: In LMN hypoglossal (CN XII) palsy, the protruded tongue deviates toward the paralysed side (with ipsilateral atrophy/fasciculation) due to the intact contralateral genioglossus.

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Sign: Tongue deviation to the side of the lesion (Left CN XII palsy in PDF variant; Right CN XII palsy in 2018 PPTX variant) due to unopposed action of the contralateral genioglossus muscle. Causes: Brainstem stroke (medial medullary syndrome), Skull-base tumour/fracture (hypoglossal canal), Trauma/iatrogenic injury (carotid endarterectomy, neck dissection), Motor neuron disease (ALS), Syringobulbia.

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Right LMN Facial Nerve Palsy Localisation
stem: A 40-year-old man is examined in the neurology clinic. He is asked first to bare his teeth (A) and then to raise his eyebrows and wrinkle his forehead (B), as shown. Which nerve and anatomical level are affected?
options: Right facial nerve (CN VII); lower motor neuron lesion
Left facial nerve (CN VII); upper motor neuron lesion
Right trigeminal nerve (CN V); motor division lesion
Left facial nerve (CN VII); lower motor neuron lesion
Right facial nerve (CN VII); upper motor neuron lesion
optionRationales: Correct: In panel A, the mouth pulls toward the intact left side while the right nasolabial fold is flattened; in panel B, the right forehead fails to wrinkle alongside the left—indicating involvement of both upper and lower right facial musculature from a right LMN CN VII lesion.
Incorrect: A left UMN lesion would weaken only the left lower face while preserving forehead wrinkling bilaterally.
Incorrect: CN V innervates the muscles of mastication and facial sensation, not facial expression or frontalis wrinkling.
Incorrect: The left side of the face contracts normally on smiling and wrinkles robustly on forehead elevation, proving the left facial nerve is intact.
Incorrect: An upper motor neuron lesion of the right face (left hemisphere stroke) would spare the right forehead because upper facial nuclei receive bilateral cortical input.
clinicalPearl: Always test forehead wrinkling (frontalis) and tight eye closure (orbicularis oculi) in facial asymmetry: forehead involvement localises the lesion to an LMN facial palsy (Bell's palsy, pontine nucleus, or CPA tumour), whereas forehead sparing indicates a contralateral UMN lesion.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Forehead involvement (loss of wrinkling) alongside lower facial paralysis distinguishes an ipsilateral LMN CN VII lesion from a contralateral UMN lesion.

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 62-year-old patient with hypertension and binocular horizontal diplopia is asked to look toward the right side, demonstrating the eye positions shown. Which cranial nerve and extraocular muscle are paralysed?
options: Right oculomotor (CN III) nerve; right medial rectus muscle
Left oculomotor (CN III) nerve; left medial rectus muscle
Left abducens (CN VI) nerve; left lateral rectus muscle
Right trochlear (CN IV) nerve; right superior oblique muscle
Right abducens (CN VI) nerve; right lateral rectus muscle
optionRationales: Incorrect: Right CN III palsy causes impaired adduction, elevation, depression, ptosis, and/or mydriasis rather than isolated failure of abduction.
Incorrect: The patient's left eye (viewer's right) adducts cleanly toward the medial canthus, proving left CN III medial rectus function is intact.
Incorrect: Left CN VI palsy impairs leftward abduction of the left eye, whereas here rightward abduction of the right eye is impaired.
Incorrect: Right CN IV palsy impairs intorsion and downward gaze in adduction (reading/descending stairs) rather than horizontal abduction.

Correct: On attempted rightward gaze (toward the viewer's left), the left eye adducts fully via the intact left medial rectus while the right eye fails to abduct laterally, diagnostic of right abducens (CN VI) palsy affecting the right lateral rectus muscle.
clinicalPearl: In CN VI palsy, horizontal diplopia is worst when looking toward the paralysed side and for distant objects; remember 'LR6 SO4 all others 3' and always inspect the fundus for papilloedema (false localising sign in raised ICP).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Failure of right eye abduction on rightward gaze indicates right abducens (CN VI) palsy (lateral rectus paralysis).

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Acute Bell's Palsy Diagnosis & First-Line Management
stem: A 30-year-old man presents within 24 hours of developing acute facial asymmetry and is photographed while attempting to close his eyes and bare his teeth. Otoscopy is normal without vesicles, and limb power is full. What is the diagnosis and optimal initial management?
options: Left upper motor neuron facial palsy; immediate non-contrast CT brain and aspirin loading
Left Bell's palsy; oral prednisolone within 72 hours plus lubricating eye drops and nocturnal taping
Right Bell's palsy; urgent surgical decompression of the right stylomastoid foramen
Left Ramsay Hunt syndrome; oral aciclovir monotherapy without systemic corticosteroids
Left parotid gland carcinoma; immediate fine-needle aspiration and radical parotidectomy
optionRationales: Incorrect: Incomplete closure of the left eye indicates LMN involvement rather than a forehead-sparing UMN stroke.

Correct: The photograph shows incomplete left eyelid closure and asymmetrical mouth pull to the right, indicating left LMN facial palsy (Bell's palsy); oral prednisolone started within 72 hours significantly improves complete recovery, and artificial tears with nocturnal taping prevent exposure keratitis.
Incorrect: The paralysed side is the left (not right), and surgical decompression is not indicated for acute uncomplicated Bell's palsy.
Incorrect: Normal otoscopy without ear vesicles rules out Ramsay Hunt syndrome, and corticosteroid therapy is the primary evidence-based treatment for Bell's palsy.
Incorrect: Acute 24-hour onset without a parotid mass points to idiopathic Bell's palsy rather than parotid malignancy (though parotid palpation should always be performed).
clinicalPearl: For CSS management marks on Bell's palsy, never omit eye protection (daytime methylcellulose drops, nocturnal ointment and eye taping/patching) to prevent corneal ulceration alongside early oral prednisolone.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Acute left LMN CN VII palsy (Bell's palsy) requires oral corticosteroids within 72 hours and corneal protection (lubrication + nocturnal taping).

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 55-year-old man with hoarseness and nasal regurgitation of liquids is asked to open his mouth and say 'Aah', revealing the oropharyngeal appearance shown. Which cranial nerve is affected, and what explains the direction of uvular deviation?
options: Right glossopharyngeal (CN IX) nerve; asymmetrical sensory afferent gag impairment
Left spinal accessory (CN XI) nerve; weakness of the ipsilateral stylopharyngeus muscle
Right vagus (CN X) nerve; unopposed upward pull of the paralysed right palatal arch
Left vagus (CN X) nerve; unopposed elevation by the intact right levator veli palatini
Left hypoglossal (CN XII) nerve; ipsilateral loss of genioglossus pharyngeal tension
optionRationales: Incorrect: CN IX supplies sensory afferents of the gag reflex and stylopharyngeus, whereas motor elevation of the soft palate (except tensor veli palatini) is mediated by CN X.
Incorrect: The spinal component of CN XI supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; palatal motor elevation depends on CN X.
Incorrect: The palate elevates robustly on the patient's right side (viewer's left) and the uvula is drawn toward that intact right side, indicating a left-sided lesion.

Correct: On phonation, the left soft palate arch fails to elevate (droops) and the uvula is pulled toward the intact right side (viewer's left) by unopposed contraction of the right levator veli palatini, diagnostic of left vagus (CN X) nerve palsy.
Incorrect: CN XII supplies intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles and does not elevate the soft palate or move the uvula.
clinicalPearl: Assess CN X comprehensively in CSS stations: check soft palate elevation ('Aah'), gag reflex (afferent CN IX, efferent CN X), voice quality (hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy), and bovine cough.

guideCitation.keyPoint: In CN X palsy, the soft palate droops on the affected side and the uvula deviates toward the intact contralateral side on saying 'Aah'.

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 28-year-old man complains of fluctuating double vision and drooping eyelids that worsen toward the evening. The top photograph shows his eyes at baseline, and the bottom photograph was taken after 3 minutes of sustained upward gaze. What is the diagnosis, and which confirmatory work-up is most appropriate?
options: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome; anti-VGCC antibodies and improvement on sustained gaze
Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy; suppressed serum TSH and elevated TRAb antibodies
Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia; single-dose edrophonium without imaging
Myasthenia gravis; anti-AChR antibodies, repetitive nerve stimulation, and CT thorax
Bilateral oculomotor nerve palsy; urgent cerebral angiography for bilateral aneurysms
optionRationales: Incorrect: Lambert-Eaton syndrome shows facilitation (transient strengthening) with repeated effort, spares extraocular muscles more often than MG, and causes autonomic features and hyporeflexia.
Incorrect: Thyroid eye disease typically produces lid retraction and proptosis rather than fatigable ptosis worsening on sustained gaze.
Incorrect: Mitochondrial CPEO presents with symmetric, slowly progressive non-fatigable external ophthalmoplegia and does not characteristically show fatigable Simpson's sign.

Correct: Progressive worsening of ptosis during sustained upward gaze demonstrates fatigable neuromuscular junction transmission (positive Simpson's test), diagnostic of myasthenia gravis; confirm with anti-AChR (or anti-MuSK) antibodies, decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation / single-fibre EMG, and CT thorax to exclude thymoma.
Incorrect: Bilateral CN III palsies produce fixed ptosis with pupillary/extraocular paralysis rather than fatigable ptosis elicited by prolonged upward gaze.
clinicalPearl: Alongside Simpson's test (fatigable ptosis on sustained upward gaze), remember the bedside ice-pack test for MG: cooling inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction, temporarily improving ptosis by >=2 mm.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Fatigable ptosis provoked by 3 minutes of upward gaze (positive Simpson's test) indicates myasthenia gravis; exclude thymoma with CT thorax.

sourceStation.title: Ocular Myasthenia Gravis (Simpson's Test)

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Myasthenia gravis (ocular/generalised) — fatigable ptosis elicited by prolonged upward gaze (positive Simpson's test). Confirm with anti-AChR / anti-MuSK antibodies, repetitive nerve stimulation (decremental response), single-fibre EMG, and CT thorax (thymoma).

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Left Abducens Nerve Palsy & False Localising Sign
stem: A 34-year-old woman with morning headaches, papilloedema, and horizontal diplopia is asked to look laterally to her left, as shown. What is the precise cranial nerve lesion, and why can raised intracranial pressure produce it?
options: Left trochlear (CN IV) palsy; compression of its dorsal midbrain exit within the ambient cistern
Right abducens (CN VI) palsy; cavernous sinus congestion selectively impairs ipsilateral abduction
Left abducens (CN VI) palsy; caudal brainstem shift stretches the nerve over the petrous ridge
Right oculomotor (CN III) palsy; uncal herniation compresses the nerve against the tentorium
Left internuclear ophthalmoplegia; demyelination of the right medial longitudinal fasciculus
optionRationales: Incorrect: Trochlear nerve palsy affects the superior oblique muscle and vertical/torsional movement rather than horizontal abduction.
Incorrect: Leftward gaze tests the left lateral rectus (left CN VI) and right medial rectus; the left eye fails to abduct here.

Correct: On leftward gaze (toward the viewer's right), the right eye adducts fully while the left eye fails to abduct laterally, indicating left CN VI palsy; because CN VI has a long intracranial course tethered at Dorello's canal, raised ICP pushes the brainstem downward and stretches it over the petrous temporal ridge (classic false localising sign).
Incorrect: The right eye adducts normally toward the nose on leftward gaze, showing intact right medial rectus (CN III) function.
Incorrect: In left INO, the *left* eye fails to adduct on rightward gaze with abducting nystagmus of the right eye, which is the opposite of impaired left abduction.
clinicalPearl: In raised ICP (e.g., idiopathic intracranial hypertension or space-occupying lesion), unilateral or bilateral CN VI palsy acts as a 'false localising sign'—always perform fundoscopy for papilloedema before attributing diplopia to a focal pontine lesion.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Left eye abduction failure on leftward gaze indicates left CN VI palsy; raised ICP stretches CN VI over the petrous ridge as a false localising sign.

sourceStation.title: Left Abducens (CN VI) Nerve Palsy on Leftward Gaze
sourceStation.originalPrompt: 3. Identify the condition precisely.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Left abducens (6th cranial) nerve palsy (demonstrated on leftward gaze: intact right medial rectus adducts fully while paralysed left lateral rectus fails to abduct the left eye; secondary over-adduction of right eye follows Hering's law).

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Retro-Orbital Swelling & Cavernous Sinus Cranial Nerves
stem: A 19-year-old man presents with high fever, severe unilateral retro-orbital pain, proptosis, and the acute periorbital swelling shown, raising concern for orbital apex and cavernous sinus extension. Assessment of which group of cranial nerves is essential to detect compressive or thrombotic involvement?
options: Trochlear (CN IV), abducens (CN VI), facial (CN VII), spinal accessory (CN XI), and hypoglossal (CN XII)
Oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), mandibular V3 (CN V), abducens (CN VI), and facial (CN VII)
Optic (CN II), oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), trigeminal V1–V2 (CN V), and abducens (CN VI)
Olfactory (CN I), optic (CN II), oculomotor (CN III), facial (CN VII), and vestibulocochlear (CN VIII)
Optic (CN II), trigeminal V1–V3 (CN V), glossopharyngeal (CN IX), vagus (CN X), and hypoglossal (CN XII)
optionRationales: Incorrect: CN VII, XI, and XII are not contents of the cavernous sinus or retro-orbital space.
Incorrect: The mandibular division (CN V3) exits via foramen ovale without entering the cavernous sinus, and CN VII does not traverse the orbit.

Correct: Retro-orbital and cavernous sinus / orbital apex pathology threatens CN II (optic canal — visual acuity/RAPD) as well as the nerves traversing the cavernous sinus and superior orbital fissure: CN III, CN IV, CN V1 (ophthalmic), CN V2 (maxillary, lateral cavernous wall), and CN VI.
Incorrect: CN I (cribriform plate), CN VII, and CN VIII (internal acoustic meatus) do not pass through the orbital apex or cavernous sinus.
Incorrect: CN V3, IX, X, and XII lie outside the orbital apex and cavernous sinus (lower cranial nerves exit via the jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal).
clinicalPearl: Cavernous sinus thrombosis classically follows mid-facial/periorbital sepsis ('danger triangle' via valveless facial-ophthalmic veins): CN VI is often affected earliest (lying freely inside the sinus next to the internal carotid artery) before CN III, IV, V1, and V2.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Retro-orbital and cavernous sinus lesions endanger CN II (orbital apex) alongside CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI.

sourceStation.title: Retro-Orbital Swelling / Cavernous Sinus Cranial Nerves
sourceStation.originalPrompt: 4. List cranial nerves that could be damaged by the retro-orbital swelling shown below.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Optic nerve (CN II) (vision loss/RAPD via orbital apex) and Cavernous sinus / Superior orbital fissure cranial nerves: Oculomotor (CN III), Trochlear (CN IV), Trigeminal ophthalmic & maxillary divisions (CN V1 & V2), and Abducens (CN VI).

domain: 1.4 ENDOCRINOLOGY & METABOLIC MEDICINE (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with palpitations, weight loss, heat intolerance, and the ocular appearance shown in the left panel (compared with post-treatment appearance on the right). What is the most likely diagnosis, and which first-line laboratory profile confirms it?
options: Ocular myasthenia gravis; normal TSH with positive anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies
Graves' disease; suppressed serum TSH with elevated free T4 and positive TRAb
Central pituitary hypothyroidism; suppressed serum TSH with low free T4
Subacute viral thyroiditis; markedly elevated serum TSH with high radioiodine uptake
Hashimoto's thyroiditis; elevated serum TSH with low free T4 and anti-TPO antibodies
optionRationales: Incorrect: Myasthenia gravis causes ptosis rather than bilateral exophthalmos and lid retraction, and does not cause heat intolerance or weight loss.

Correct: Bilateral exophthalmos (proptosis) with lid retraction and scleral show alongside hyperthyroid symptoms is pathognomonic for Graves' disease, confirmed biochemically by suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/total T3, and positive TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb).
Incorrect: Central hypothyroidism produces low free T4 alongside low/inappropriately normal TSH and does not cause proptosis or thyrotoxicosis.
Incorrect: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis causes painful tender goitre, suppressed TSH during the early phase, and *low* radioiodine uptake without true Graves' orbitopathy.
Incorrect: Hashimoto's thyroiditis typically causes primary hypothyroidism (high TSH, low free T4) rather than hyperthyroidism with Graves' orbitopathy.
clinicalPearl: Remember the three classic extrathyroidal autoimmune manifestations unique to Graves' disease (absent in toxic multinodular goitre): Graves' orbitopathy (exophthalmos, lid lag/retraction), pretibial myxoedema, and thyroid acropachy.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Graves' disease presents with bilateral exophthalmos/lid retraction and is confirmed by suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/T3, and positive TRAb.

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Graves' disease (Hyperthyroidism). Investigations: Serum TSH (suppressed/low) and Free T4 / Total T3 & T4 (elevated); TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb) / TPO antibodies; Radioiodine uptake scan / Thyroid ultrasound.

domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
topic: Acute Pericarditis vs STEMI ECG Differentiation
stem: A 29-year-old man presents with sharp central chest pain that worsens on deep inspiration and lying flat, and eases when leaning forward. His 12-lead ECG shows widespread upward-concave ST-segment elevation across precordial and limb leads without reciprocal ST depression. Which additional ECG feature strongly supports acute pericarditis over an acute myocardial infarction?
options: Diffuse PR-segment depression accompanied by PR-segment elevation in lead aVR
Deep symmetrical T-wave inversions with markedly prolonged QTc interval
Convex tombstone ST-segment elevation strictly confined to leads V1–V4
Tall broad R waves and horizontal ST-segment depression in leads V1–V2
Pathological Q waves in leads II, III, and aVF with ST depression in lead aVL
optionRationales: Correct: Per the ECG Reference Guide, acute pericarditis classically causes diffuse concave ST-segment elevation, no reciprocal ST depression, and PR-segment depression across most leads with reciprocal PR-segment elevation in lead aVR.
Incorrect: Deep symmetrical T-wave inversions with QTc prolongation (Wellens/ischaemic or Takotsubo pattern) point to myocardial ischaemia or stress cardiomyopathy rather than pericarditis.
Incorrect: Regional convex ST elevation confined to V1–V4 indicates acute anteroseptal STEMI rather than generalised pericardial inflammation.
Incorrect: Tall R waves with horizontal ST depression in V1–V2 represent acute posterior STEMI.
Incorrect: Inferior pathological Q waves with reciprocal ST depression in aVL reflect acute or established inferior myocardial infarction.
clinicalPearl: Per the Kelaniya ECG Reference Guide, up to 43% of true STEMIs can show subtle concave STE early on—so always check for PR-segment depression, absence of reciprocal ST depression, and serial ECGs at 5–10 minute intervals when in doubt.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Acute pericarditis causes diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression (PR elevation in aVR), and no reciprocal ST depression.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 54-year-old man who worked in an asbestos roofing-sheet factory for 18 years presents with progressively worsening exertional dyspnoea. Chest radiography demonstrates bilateral calcified pleural plaques and diaphragmatic calcifications, and HRCT reveals basal honeycombing. Which spirometric pattern and malignancy risk are characteristic of his condition?
options: Reduced FEV₁ and FVC with normal or elevated FEV₁/FVC ratio; malignant mesothelioma
Isolated reduction in peak expiratory flow with normal lung volumes; mediastinal thymoma
Reduced FEV₁ with normal FVC and FEV₁/FVC ratio below 0.70; small cell carcinoma
Increased total lung capacity with elevated DLCO; pulmonary chondroid hamartoma
Marked bronchodilator reversibility above 12% in FEV₁; bronchial carcinoid tumour
optionRationales: Correct: Per the CSS CXR Guide (Item 7), asbestosis causes restrictive lung physiology—reduction of both FEV₁ and FVC so the FEV₁/FVC ratio remains normal or >=70%—along with basal honeycombing, pleural/diaphragmatic calcifications, and high risk of malignant mesothelioma (as well as bronchogenic carcinoma).
Incorrect: Asbestosis reduces total lung volumes (TLC, FVC, FEV₁) and is linked to mesothelioma and lung carcinoma, not thymoma.
Incorrect: An FEV₁/FVC ratio <0.70 defines obstructive lung disease (such as COPD/asthma) rather than restrictive interstitial fibrosis.
Incorrect: Interstitial lung disease reduces total lung capacity and *lowers* (not elevates) DLCO, and hamartomas present as solitary nodules with 'popcorn' calcification.
Incorrect: Bronchodilator reversibility >12% and >200 mL characterises bronchial asthma rather than asbestos-related pulmonary fibrosis.
clinicalPearl: In Sri Lankan CXR OSCEs, remember the classic occupational pairing: asbestos sheet factory -> diaphragmatic calcifications + pleural plaques + lower-zone honeycombing + restrictive spirometry (FEV₁/FVC >=70%) + mesothelioma risk (whereas silicosis gives upper-zone fibrosis and 'eggshell' hilar nodes).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Asbestosis produces pleural/diaphragmatic calcifications, basal honeycombing, restrictive spirometry (FEV1/FVC >=70%), and mesothelioma risk.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
topic: Serial ABG Interpretation in Acute Asthma Exhaustion
stem: A 25-year-old woman with acute severe asthma arrives alert and tachypnoeic with an initial ABG showing pH 7.48, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, PaO₂ 68 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 24 mmol/L. Despite nebulised bronchodilators and oxygen, a repeat ABG 1 hour later shows pH 7.33, PaCO₂ 45 mmHg, PaO₂ 80 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 24 mmol/L, with reduced wheezing and drowsiness. How should this PaCO₂ trend be interpreted?
options: Onset of respiratory muscle exhaustion indicating life-threatening asthma requiring urgent ICU review
Inadvertent arterialisation of a venous sample with no change in ventilatory status
Renal compensation for acute hyperventilation confirming resolution of bronchospasm
Normalisation of ventilation confirming a favourable response to nebulised beta-2 agonist therapy
Primary metabolic alkalosis precipitated by repeated systemic corticosteroid administration
optionRationales: Correct: As highlighted in the CSS Blood Gas Analysis Guide, acutely breathless asthmatics initially hyperventilate and blow off CO₂ (PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, respiratory alkalosis). A rising PaCO₂ trend into the 'normal' or mildly elevated range (45 mmHg, pH 7.33) accompanied by a silent chest/drowsiness signifies respiratory muscle exhaustion and impending arrest.
Incorrect: Venous sampling does not explain clinical deterioration (drowsiness and reduced breath sounds/silent chest) alongside acute hypercapnic acidaemia.
Incorrect: Renal compensation lowers HCO₃⁻ slowly over days rather than elevating PaCO₂ over 1 hour.
Incorrect: Interpreting a 'normal' PaCO₂ of 45 mmHg in an exhausted asthmatic as reassuring improvement is a classic fatal error.
Incorrect: The pH has fallen from 7.48 to acidaemic 7.33 due to rising PaCO₂ (respiratory acidosis), not metabolic alkalosis.
clinicalPearl: Never be falsely reassured by a 'normal' PaCO₂ (35–45 mmHg) in an acute severe asthma attack—compare serial blood gases! A rising PaCO₂ + silent chest + exhaustion = life-threatening asthma requiring IV magnesium/aminophylline and urgent ICU/anaesthetic alert.

guideCitation.keyPoint: In acute severe asthma, a rising trend in PaCO2 (even into the 'normal' range) indicates ventilatory muscle exhaustion and life-threatening asthma.

domain: 1.4 ENDOCRINOLOGY & METABOLIC MEDICINE (12 STATIONS)
topic: High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis & ABG Analysis
stem: A 25-year-old woman is admitted drowsy after 3 days of polyuria, thirst, and dysuria. On room air, her ABG shows pH 7.20, PaCO₂ 24 mmHg, PaO₂ 100 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L, and base excess −18 mmol/L; serum Na⁺ is 136 mmol/L, K⁺ 4.8 mmol/L, and Cl⁻ 100 mmol/L. Which acid-base disturbance is present, and what drives the anion gap?
options: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation; renal bicarbonate wasting
Primary respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation; sepsis-driven hyperventilation
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation; accumulation of ketoacids
Mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis; alveolar hypoventilation with chloride retention
Uncompensated metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap; gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss
optionRationales: Incorrect: In normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) acidosis, serum chloride rises proportionally as HCO₃⁻ falls so the anion gap remains normal (~10–14 mmol/L with K⁺), unlike the markedly elevated gap here.
Incorrect: The arterial pH is severely acidaemic (7.20), whereas primary respiratory alkalosis produces alkalaemia (pH >7.45).

Correct: A low pH (7.20), low HCO₃⁻ (10 mmol/L), and markedly negative base excess (−18 mmol/L) define primary metabolic acidosis; PaCO₂ has fallen appropriately to 24 mmHg via Kussmaul hyperventilation (Winter's formula: 1.5 × 10 + 8 = 23 ± 2 mmHg), and the anion gap (Na⁺ + K⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = 30.8 mmol/L is elevated by unmeasured ketoacids in DKA.
Incorrect: PaCO₂ is appropriately suppressed to 24 mmHg (hyperventilation), ruling out concomitant respiratory acidosis.
Incorrect: Compensatory hyperventilation has lowered PaCO₂ to 24 mmHg, and the calculated anion gap is substantially elevated rather than normal.
clinicalPearl: Per the Kelaniya ABG Guide, base excess and standard HCO₃⁻ quantify the metabolic component independently of acute PaCO₂ changes, while the anion gap (Na⁺ + K⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) separates keto/lactic acidosis from hyperchloraemic diarrhoea/RTA.

guideCitation.keyPoint: High anion gap metabolic acidosis reduces HCO3- via addition of unmeasured anions (e.g. ketoacids, lactate), whereas normal anion gap acidosis raises Cl-.

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Glasgow Coma Scale Scoring & Head Injury Severity
stem: A 42-year-old motorcyclist is brought to the Emergency Treatment Unit after a road traffic collision. On examination, he opens his eyes only to firm nail-bed pressure, produces incomprehensible groaning sounds without intelligible words, and demonstrates abnormal slow flexion of both elbows across his chest to painful stimulation. What is his total GCS score and head injury classification?
options: GCS 7/15 (E1 V3 M3); moderate head injury
GCS 7/15 (E2 V2 M3); severe head injury
GCS 9/15 (E3 V2 M4); moderate head injury
GCS 8/15 (E2 V2 M4); severe head injury
GCS 6/15 (E2 V2 M2); severe head injury
optionRationales: Incorrect: E1 is no eye opening at all and V3 is inappropriate words; furthermore, a total GCS of 7 is classified as severe (<=8), not moderate (9–12).

Correct: Per the CSS GCS Guide, eye opening to peripheral pain scores E2, incomprehensible sounds score V2, and abnormal flexion (decorticate posturing) scores M3, giving a total of 7/15; a GCS of 8 or less defines coma and severe head injury.
Incorrect: E3 represents eye opening to verbal command rather than to pain (E2), and M4 represents withdrawal rather than abnormal flexion.
Incorrect: M4 represents normal purposeful withdrawal away from a painful stimulus rather than stereotyped abnormal decorticate flexion (M3).
Incorrect: M2 represents abnormal extension (decerebrate posturing), whereas slow flexion of the elbows across the chest is M3.
clinicalPearl: Key rules from the Kelaniya GCS OSCE Guide: never apply painful stimuli to the face when testing eye opening (use trapezius pinch or nail-bed pressure), record the best motor response across limbs, and remember 'GCS <= 8 = coma / severe head injury — consider intubation'.

guideCitation.keyPoint: GCS classification: Severe <=8 (Coma), Moderate 9–12, Mild 13–15; abnormal flexion (decorticate) = M3 and eye opening to non-facial pain = E2.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
topic: Metered-Dose Inhaler & Spacer Device Technique and Care
stem: A 46-year-old man with moderate persistent asthma is prescribed a beclomethasone dipropionate metered-dose inhaler (MDI) used with a large-volume plastic spacer. Which instruction regarding inhaler use and spacer maintenance is essential to maximise lung deposition and prevent local side effects?
options: Inhale as fast and forcefully as possible as soon as the MDI canister is depressed into the spacer
Actuate two puffs together into the spacer chamber before taking one deep breath-hold
Place the disassembled spacer halves in direct midday sunlight weekly for rapid thermal sterilisation
Wipe the inside of the plastic chamber dry with a clean cloth after washing to clear static droplets
Clean with lukewarm water, air-dry in the shade without wiping the inside, and rinse mouth after use
optionRationales: Incorrect: Fast, forceful inhalation is required for dry powder inhalers (DPIs) to de-aggregate powder; an MDI/spacer requires a slow, steady, deep inhalation followed by a 10-second breath-hold.
Incorrect: Actuating multiple puffs into a spacer simultaneously causes aerosol collision and rain-out inside the chamber, markedly reducing the delivered dose; always administer one puff at a time.
Incorrect: Drying a spacer in direct sunlight warps plastic components and degrades valve integrity; always air-dry in a shaded, ventilated area.

Incorrect: Rubbing or towel-drying the interior of a plastic spacer damages its antistatic property and creates static charge that attracts drug particles onto the walls instead of reaching the lungs.

Correct: Per the CSS Inhalers & Spacer Guide, washing the spacer every 2 weeks in lukewarm water (with mild detergent) and air-drying in the shade without rubbing the interior preserves its antistatic lining, while rinsing and gargling after steroid inhalation prevents oral candidiasis and dysphonia.
clinicalPearl: High-yield CSS spacer viva points: spacers evaporate propellant to reduce particle size and trap large particles—slashing oropharyngeal candidiasis and dysphonia—provided you actuate 1 puff at a time and never rub the inside dry.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Wash plastic spacers in lukewarm water and air-dry in the shade without rubbing inside (preserves antistatic lining); actuate 1 puff at a time and rinse mouth after ICS.
